conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past week since your baby arrived.  

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me otherwise, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go one question at a time, and if anything feels uncomfortable you can let me know or skip it.  

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first question:  

Over the last seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—would you say always, most of the time, sometimes, or hardly ever?

Most of the time, I guess. I still laugh when my partner makes silly faces at the baby or when the dog does something goofy. It’s not quite as automatic as before I was pregnant, but the giggles do come.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, like I said, most of the time I can still laugh—maybe not quite as loudly or easily as before, but the funny moments are still there.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Most of the time I still do. I’ll catch myself getting excited about little outings—like taking the baby for a walk to the park or having coffee on the porch—though sometimes I’m too tired to follow through. Still, the looking-forward part is usually there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Hardly ever, really. If the baby’s fussy or I’m running late, I figure it’s just part of learning how to be a mom—I don’t beat myself up over it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll suddenly worry that the baby’s breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie in bed replaying whether I buckled the car seat right—even when everything turned out fine. It’s not constant, but it pops up a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes—like yesterday, I was folding laundry and suddenly felt my heart race and this wave of “something bad is about to happen.” It passed in a minute or two, but it left me a little shaky. I knew it wasn’t logical, but I couldn’t stop it.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes. There are moments—like when the baby’s crying and the dishes are piled up—when I feel a bit overwhelmed, but I take a breath and remind myself it’s okay to tackle one thing at a time. It passes pretty quickly.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, not at all. Once I finally lie down, I’m out pretty quickly and stay asleep—unless the baby wakes me, of course. I haven’t felt so unhappy that it kept me up.
I have felt sad or miserable
Sometimes. I’ll get a little teary for no clear reason—like when a lullaby comes on—but it lifts within a few minutes. It’s not an all-day gloom, just short waves that pass.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Hardly ever. Maybe once or twice in the past week I teared up for a moment, but it stopped almost right away, and it wasn’t that deep, heavy kind of crying—just a quick blip.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
Never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared that, overall, you're still able to enjoy funny moments and look forward to small outings, even if your energy to follow through is lower right now. You described occasional, brief waves of <sym>sadness</sym> or tearing up that pass quickly, and a few times a day you notice <sym>worries</sym> about the baby's safety that intrude even when everything is fine. A single, short-lived <sym>panic-type episode</sym> left you shaky, yet you're not feeling undue <sym>guilt</sym> and you're sleeping whenever the baby lets you. Most importantly, you've had no thoughts of harming yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 10, Risk Level: Depression possible (concerns include <sym>Patient describes specific, recurring worries several times daily that intrude despite no real danger, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a sudden, unprovoked panic episode that fits "sometimes" frequency.</sym>, <sym>Acknowledges feeling overwhelmed at times but able to regain control, aligning with 'sometimes not coping as well as usual'.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 10 falls in the 9-11 range indicating possible <med>postpartum depression</med> or <med>anxiety</med>. While you retain capacity for pleasure and laugh most of the time, you report several episodes of <sym>unprompted worry</sym> and one <sym>panic attack</sym> in the past week, plus short-lived <sym>tearfulness</sym>. These features do not currently meet full <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> (which requires ≥5 symptoms for two weeks including either depressed mood or loss of interest, plus functional impairment), but they do warrant closer monitoring and supportive measures. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule a re-screen with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> in 2-3 weeks to track any changes
2. Practice 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>worries</sym> spike; pair these with daily stroller walks for light exercise and mood boost
3. Aim for at least one 4-hour block of uninterrupted sleep per 24-hours-ask your partner or support person to handle a feeding while you rest
4. Share today's results with a trusted family member so they can help watch for worsening mood, <sym>panic</sym>, or new <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym>
5. Keep the national Postpartum Support International helpline number saved (1-800-944-4773) for 24/7 emotional support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 10: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms:
- Episodic, low-grade sadness/tearfulness ("sometimes…short waves that pass")
- Preserved capacity for pleasure and anticipatory enjoyment, though energy to follow through reduced
- Intermittent, intrusive worries about infant safety; 2–3× daily, not meeting panic frequency
- Brief, self-limited panic-type episode (no avoidance or persistent anticipatory anxiety)
- Denies guilt, self-blame, sleep-mood link, or any self-harm ideation

Pattern: sub-syndromal mood and anxiety symptoms; coping strategies intact; no safety concerns identified.

Screening significance: mild postpartum anxiety with reactive mood lability; does not currently meet threshold for major depressive episode. Recommend routine re-screen in 2–3 weeks and psychoeducation on stress management/sleep.
